summary: Defines MIB objects for managing RS-232-like hardware devices using SMIv2. It is a draft standard.

eli5.summary: Gauges for checking the old-style serial ports on a computer.

questions: which snmp objects manage serial ports
how do i read modem signals with snmp
subtitle: SNMP objects for watching and setting up serial ports: speeds, framing, flow control and modem signals.

tldr.problem: Network devices have serial ports (RS-232, V.35 and similar), and managers had no standard SNMP objects for their speed, character settings, error counts or modem control signals.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an SMIv2 MIB module, rs232, with a general port table, asynchronous and synchronous port tables, and input and output control signal tables, plus compliance groups.
tldr.outcome: It is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1317. It models the physical layer, so higher-layer MIBs such as the Character MIB sit on top of it.

facts.value: other, rs232, rs422, rs423, v35, x21

sections.title: What the MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 1659 defines an extension to the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing RS-232-like hardware devices. It was written by the IETF Character MIB Working Group and obsoletes RFC 1317.

The MIB applies to interface ports that might logically support the Interface MIB, a Transmission MIB, or the Character MIB. The most common example is an RS-232 port with modem signals. It covers RS-232, RS-422, RS-423, V.35 and other asynchronous or synchronous serial physical links with a similar set of control signals.

It is mandatory for all systems that have such a hardware port supporting services managed through some other MIB.
sections.eli5: It is a list of gauges for the old-style plug on the back of a machine that sends data one bit at a time. Any machine with such a plug has to offer these gauges.

sections.title: The SNMPv2 Framework Behind It
sections.content:
The RFC builds on the SNMPv2 Network Management Framework, which has four parts: RFC 1442 (the SMI, which describes and names objects), STD 17 (RFC 1213, MIB-II, the core set of managed objects), RFC 1445 (administrative and architectural aspects) and RFC 1448 (the protocol used to reach managed objects).

Managed objects live in a virtual information store, the MIB. Each object type is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, an administratively assigned name, and is defined with the subset of ASN.1 that the SMI allows. The module itself is placed at transmission 33.
sections.eli5: Every gauge gets a unique name in a giant phone book of gauges. The manager looks a gauge up by name and reads it.

sections.title: Layering and the Interface MIB
sections.content:
The RS-232-like MIB is one of several MIBs designed for layered use, as described in the Interface MIB (RFC 1573). It normally sits in the lowest interface sublayer: it represents the physical layer and serves higher layers such as the Character MIB (RFC 1658) or the PPP MIB (RFC 1471).

The Interface MIB's ifTestTable and ifRcvAddressTable are not relevant here. The MIB is relevant for ifType values rs232(33), v35(45) and perhaps others, and it requires the conformance groups ifGeneralGroup and ifFixedLengthGroup.

The value of ifSpeed is the same as rs232PortOutSpeed. The usefulness of the error counters depends on the octet counters in ifFixedLengthGroup.
sections.eli5: Think of a building: this MIB describes the ground floor, the actual wires. Other MIBs describe the floors built on top of it.

sections.title: The Tables
sections.content:
The MIB has one base object, rs232Number (how many ports there are, whatever their state), and four tables.

  • rs232PortTable: one row per port, for all kinds of ports. It holds the port type (other, rs232, rs422, rs423, v35, x21), the counts of input and output signals, the input and output speeds in bits per second, and the input and output flow control type.
  • rs232AsyncPortTable: settings and error counters for asynchronous ports. Entries need not exist for synchronous ports.
  • rs232SyncPortTable: settings and error counters for synchronous ports.
  • rs232InSigTable and rs232OutSigTable: one row per port and signal for input and output control signals.

Rows are indexed by InterfaceIndex, the same value as ifIndex. The RFC says that by convention, and if possible, hardware port numbers map directly to external connectors, and each value must remain constant at least from one re-initialization of the network management agent to the next.
sections.eli5: There is one big table with a row for each plug, and a few helper tables with extra details: one for plugs that talk on their own timing, one for plugs that follow a shared clock, and two for the little signal lights.

sections.title: Port Settings and Error Counters
sections.content:
In the general table, rs232PortInSpeed and rs232PortOutSpeed are read-write, in bits per second. The RFC notes that non-standard values, such as 9612, are probably not allowed on most implementations. Input and output flow control types are none, ctsRts or dsrDtr, meaning no flow control at this level or use of the named hardware signals.

For asynchronous ports, the writable settings are bits per character (5 to 8), stop bits (one, two, oneAndHalf, dynamic), parity (none, odd, even, mark, space) and autobaud. When autobaud is enabled a port may sense different values for speed, parity and character size, so a manager may temporarily see values different from what it set. Three counters tally characters with parity, framing and overrun errors since system re-initialization, while the port state was up or test.

For synchronous ports, the objects include the clock source (internal, external or split, where split means an internal transmit clock and an external receive clock) and counters for frame check errors, transmit underruns, receive overruns, frames interrupted by loss of modem signals, and aborted frames.
sections.eli5: Some settings are like the rules of a conversation: how fast to talk, how many beats per word, whether to add a check beat. The counters are tally marks for each time a word was garbled.

sections.title: Synchronous SDLC Options
sections.content:
A further group of synchronous objects is meant for ports running SDLC. Each has a default value in the module.

  • rs232SyncPortRole: dte or dce (default dce).
  • rs232SyncPortEncoding: nrz or nrzi (default nrz).
  • rs232SyncPortRTSControl: controlled or constant (default constant). In controlled mode a DTE asserts RTS when it has data and waits for CTS; a DCE issues CTS only after receiving RTS and waiting out the delay.
  • rs232SyncPortRTSCTSDelay: milliseconds a DCE waits before asserting CTS (default 0), there to support older devices that cannot recognize CTS within a certain interval after asserting RTS.
  • rs232SyncPortMode: fdx, hdx, simplex-receive or simplex-send (default fdx).
  • rs232SyncPortIdlePattern: mark or space (default space).
  • rs232SyncPortMinFlags: minimum flag patterns needed to tell one frame from the next; plausible values are 1 and 2 (default 2).
sections.eli5: These are extra switches for a particular style of line: which side acts as the computer and which as the modem, how to send ones and zeros, and what the line looks like when nobody is talking.

sections.title: Control Signals
sections.content:
The input and output signal tables expose the hardware control signals. The signal name is one of eleven values, defined with reference to EIA Standard RS-232-C, August 1969: rts (Request to Send), cts (Clear to Send), dsr (Data Set Ready), dtr (Data Terminal Ready), ri (Ring Indicator), dcd (Received Line Signal Detector), sq (Signal Quality Detector), srs (Data Signaling Rate Selector), srts, scts and sdcd (the secondary variants).

Each row gives the current state (none, on or off) and a counter of how many times the signal changed from on to off or from off to on. Tables contain entries only for signals the software can detect (input) or assert (output) and that are useful to observe.
sections.eli5: The signals are tiny lights on the cable saying things like I am ready or I have something to send. The table tells you whether each light is on and how often it has flickered.

sections.title: Compliance and Security
sections.content:
The compliance statement makes rs232Group mandatory for all entities with RS-232-like hardware interfaces. The asynchronous group is mandatory only for entities with asynchronous interfaces, and the synchronous group only for those with synchronous interfaces. A separate SDLC group collects the SDLC-specific synchronous objects.

The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.eli5: Every machine with a serial plug must offer the basic gauges. Only machines with the right kind of plug must offer the extra ones. The RFC does not talk about security.
